newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Moslem party forms pact for local vote.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslem party forms pact for local vote.

text.p: The main Moslem political party in Bosnia said on Saturday it had formed a coalition with several opposition parties to contest municipal elections scheduled later this year.
Alija Izetbegovic, leader of the Party of Democratic Action (SDA), announced the coalition saying his party would only succeed in the local elections if it was "broad-minded".

"We will win if we are a true democratic alternative, if we are not a narrow rightist party, not a selective one but sufficiently broad-minded to accept all the people who wish Bosnia well..." Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the country's collective presidency, told reporters.
After more than three years of war, three nationalist parties representing Moslem, Serb and Croat communities rule Bosnia-Herzegovina.
The SDA and Croat and Serb nationalist parties prevailed in national elections held last September.
The municipal vote, which will determine the fate of towns contested during the 1992-95 war, is scheduled for September 13-14.

State media said the coalition was comprised of the SDA, the Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Liberal Bosniak Organisation, and two smaller parties -- the Liberal Party and the Civic Democratic Party.
None of the parties enjoy strong support from Bosnian Serb or Croat voters.
The Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina is led by the Moslem co-prime minister of the new central government, Haris Silajdzic.
A former SDA member, Silajdzic served as wartime prime minister and worked closely with Izetbegovic, former Bosnian president.
Political analysts say the opposition party that could potentially broaden the SDA's support is the Liberal Bosniak (Moslem) Organisation, led by a former ally of Izetbegovic.
Mohammed Filipovic, leader of the LBO, helped found the SDA with Izetbegovic but later accused some SDA members of pushing for the division of Bosnia along ethnic lines.
Izetbegovic indicated he was not impressed with some SDA politicians serving at the local level and encouraged voters to reject anyone who they did not trust.
"It still seems to me that the people deserve better authorities than us," Izetbegovic said.
"Do not elect people who lost your trust because of any reason. You will not do a favour to them or to the party."
Recent local elections in neighbouring Croatia and Yugoslavia had shown that ruling parties cannot take municipal polls for granted, he added.
